QF.id: AIFM CII Fund Monitoring Reporting and Exit_1

question.text: Ms. Meera Subramanian, an LP in Lotus Capital Cat II AIF, asks her GP how 'fund monitoring' differs from 'fund management' for her Cat I/II commitment. Which description is correct under the SEBI (AIF) framework?

answer.text: Fund monitoring is an oversight activity by investors over asset allocation, portfolio composition, governance and performance; fund management is carried out by the Manager per the contribution agreement with no LP involvement.
Fund monitoring and fund management are synonyms — LPs can direct day-to-day investment decisions once monitoring begins.
Fund monitoring is the daily NAV-striking process performed by the fund accountant; fund management is the back-office role of the trustee.
Fund monitoring is a regulatory audit conducted only by SEBI annually; fund management refers to pitch decks prepared during fund-raising.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 12, fund monitoring is an oversight process by investors on asset allocation, portfolio composition, fund governance and performance — and is expressly distinct from fund management, in which (per the contribution agreement) investors have NO involvement. The Manager runs the fund; LPs monitor. The Trap: Option B conflates oversight with control — LPs in a blind-pool AIF never direct picks. Option C mixes a Cat III daily NAV mechanic into a Cat I/II question. Option D invents a non-existent 'SEBI annual audit' role. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A (Cat I/II Distributor) frames this from the investor-sales side. XIX-C covers all-cat managers. XIX-D (this exam) tests the Cat I/II Manager desk's duty to RESPECT monitoring boundaries while delivering reporting. Manager's Pro-Tip: On the GP desk, volunteer LP Advisory Committee (LPAC) meetings and a standing quarterly portfolio review even when not contractually forced — LPs whose monitoring appetite is fed stay committed to Fund II and Fund III.
